fields.definition: A positive tonal descriptor for the presence of clean, extended high-frequency content, roughly above 10 kHz, that lends a recording air, brilliance and fine detail without edginess or harshness.
fields.plain_english: A sparkling sound has clear, airy highs, like the shimmer of a cymbal or a small bell. It sounds bright and full of detail, but not harsh.
fields.purpose_function: It communicates a desirable sense of top-end openness and detail, guiding EQ and microphone choices toward capturing or restoring high-frequency air.
fields.practical_application: An engineer adds sparkle with a gentle high-shelf boost around 10 to 15 kHz, an air-band EQ, or a brighter condenser mic on sources such as acoustic guitar, cymbals or vocals.
common_mistakes: Confusing pleasant sparkle with harshness or sibilance, then boosting highs until the sound turns edgy
Adding high-frequency boost to a dull source that lacks the content, only raising hiss and noise
Assuming more sparkle is always better, ignoring how excess top end fatigues listeners
scenario_contexts: A producer asks for more sparkle on an acoustic guitar so it cuts through a dense mix
Restoring air to a dull vocal recorded with a dark microphone
Adding shimmer to drum overheads so cymbals sound open and detailed

sources: Bobby Owsinski, The Mixing Engineer's Handbook

fields.definition: A negative tonal descriptor for a harsh, spitting quality in the upper-midrange and high frequencies, typically exaggerated sibilance or plosive and transient artifacts in the region of roughly 4 to 8 kHz.
fields.plain_english: A spitty sound has harsh, spitting 'sss' and 'tss' noises in the highs. It often comes from too much treble, a cheap mic, or heavy data compression.
fields.purpose_function: It flags an unpleasant, aggressive top-end fault so it can be tamed, pointing the engineer toward de-essing or a narrow EQ cut.
fields.practical_application: A technician who hears spitty consonants on a vocal applies a de-esser or a narrow cut around 5 to 8 kHz, swaps a harsh microphone, or checks for lossy-codec artifacts.
common_mistakes: Fixing spittiness with a broad high cut that dulls the whole sound instead of a narrow, targeted cut
Over-de-essing until the vocal lisps and loses clarity
Blaming the mic when the real cause is a plosive pop or a lossy codec artifact
scenario_contexts: A lead vocal sounds spitty on loud 's' and 't' sounds and needs de-essing
A speech track through an aggressive codec develops a spitty high end
A cheap condenser makes an already bright singer sound spitty in the presence range

sources: Bobby Owsinski, The Mixing Engineer's Handbook

fields.definition: A negative tonal descriptor for an uncontrolled, distorted or smeared transient, most often on drums or cymbals, where the attack splatters rather than staying focused; commonly a symptom of over-compression, clipping or overdriven transients.
fields.plain_english: A splatty sound is when a drum hit smears out instead of staying sharp and clean. It usually means the sound was pushed too hard or squashed too much.
fields.purpose_function: It identifies a loss of transient control or the onset of distortion so the engineer can back off compression, gain or limiting.
fields.practical_application: When a snare or cymbal sounds splatty, a technician lowers compressor ratio or input gain, checks for clipping in the chain, and restores a cleaner, more defined attack.
common_mistakes: Pushing a limiter or clipper too hard on drums until transients splatter and lose punch
Mistaking gain-stage clipping for a creative effect and leaving audible distortion in the mix
Over-compressing the drum bus so every hit smears together
scenario_contexts: A heavily limited drum bus makes snare hits sound splatty on loud sections
Cymbals distort and splatter after too much brickwall limiting in mastering
An overdriven preamp adds a splatty edge to a close-miked snare

sources: Bobby Owsinski, The Mixing Engineer's Handbook

fields.definition: A tonal descriptor, usually mildly negative, for a sound that is technically clean and accurate but lacks warmth, harmonic richness or emotional character; often associated with clinical, over-processed or early digital reproduction.
fields.plain_english: A sterile sound is very clean but cold and lifeless. It is correct, yet it lacks warmth and feeling, like a room with no character.
fields.purpose_function: It signals that a source or system, though free of obvious faults, feels lifeless, prompting the addition of warmth, saturation or ambience.
fields.practical_application: To counter a sterile mix, an engineer may add analogue-style saturation, subtle harmonic distortion, room ambience or gentle low-mid warmth to reintroduce character.
common_mistakes: Chasing so much technical cleanliness that the mix ends up sterile and dull
Treating all added harmonics or noise as faults to remove, stripping out useful character
Confusing a sterile source with an accurate, neutral monitor and 'fixing' the monitoring instead
scenario_contexts: A fully in-the-box mix sounds sterile and the producer wants analogue warmth added
An early digital recording feels sterile compared with its tape counterpart
A vocal captured in a dead, dry booth sounds sterile and needs ambience

sources: Bobby Owsinski, The Mixing Engineer's Handbook

fields.definition: A common studio instruction to reduce excess low-midrange energy, typically in the region of roughly 200 to 500 Hz, that makes a source or mix sound muddy, boxy or congested; usually accomplished with an EQ cut in that band.
fields.plain_english: This means cutting the low-middle tones that make a mix sound thick and cloudy. Doing this helps each part sound clearer.
fields.purpose_function: It directs the engineer to clear low-mid buildup so individual parts gain definition and the mix sounds more open.
fields.practical_application: A technician sweeps a narrow EQ boost to find the offending frequency around 250 to 400 Hz, then cuts it on guitars, piano or the mix bus to take the mud out.
common_mistakes: Cutting too much low-mid so the sound becomes thin and loses warmth and body
Cutting the same 300 Hz band on every track, hollowing out the whole mix
Trying to fix muddiness with more high boost instead of removing the low-mid cause
scenario_contexts: A dense rock mix sounds muddy and the producer says to take the mud out of the rhythm guitars
A boomy vocal recorded close to a mic needs low-mids cut for clarity
A piano masks the bass, so the engineer clears low-mid mud to separate them

sources: Bobby Owsinski, The Mixing Engineer's Handbook

fields.definition: A negative tonal descriptor for a sound lacking low-frequency and low-mid body or fundamental energy, so it seems weak, lightweight and lacking fullness; the opposite of full, warm or fat.
fields.plain_english: A thin sound is missing its low notes and body, so it feels weak and small. It is like a voice heard through a cheap phone speaker.
fields.purpose_function: It flags a deficiency of low-end weight so the engineer can add body, adjust mic placement, or ease off excessive high-pass filtering.
fields.practical_application: When a guitar or vocal sounds thin, a technician boosts low-mids around 100 to 250 Hz, moves the mic closer for proximity effect, or backs off an aggressive low cut.
common_mistakes: High-passing too aggressively on every channel until sources sound thin
Confusing a thin source with good clarity and leaving it weak in the mix
Adding low-mid boost to fix thinness until the sound becomes muddy instead
scenario_contexts: A DI electric guitar sounds thin and needs low-mid weight added
A vocal recorded far from the mic loses body and sounds thin
Over-aggressive low cuts on a live console leave the whole band sounding thin

sources: Bobby Owsinski, The Mixing Engineer's Handbook

fields.definition: A tonal descriptor for a sound dominated by a strong, emphasized low-frequency thump or punch, typically the impact of a kick drum or bass in the region of roughly 50 to 100 Hz; positive when it means solid punch, negative when it means boomy or one-note.
fields.plain_english: A thumpy sound has a strong, heavy low punch, like the thud of a kick drum you feel in your chest.
fields.purpose_function: It describes the weight and impact of the low end, guiding decisions about kick and bass level, EQ and dynamics.
fields.practical_application: An engineer may EQ a kick to be more thumpy by boosting around 60 to 80 Hz, or tame an over-thumpy low end that is masking the bass and clouding the mix.
common_mistakes: Boosting kick thump so much it masks the bass guitar and muddies the low end
Judging thump on small speakers that cannot reproduce those frequencies
Confusing useful thump with uncontrolled room boom or resonance
scenario_contexts: A dance kick needs to be thumpy so listeners feel it on a club system
A live kick drum sounds too thumpy and boomy and needs low-end control
Adding thump to a lightweight kick to give it more impact in a rock mix

sources: Bobby Owsinski, The Mixing Engineer's Handbook

fields.definition: A positive tonal descriptor for a well-controlled, focused low end and transients with no boom, ringing or sloppy decay; also applied to rhythmic precision where parts lock cleanly together.
fields.plain_english: A tight sound has a firm, controlled low end with no boom or ringing. The notes start and stop cleanly.
fields.purpose_function: It signals control and definition in the low end and timing, guiding EQ, damping, gating and dynamics choices toward a clean, focused result.
fields.practical_application: A technician tightens low end by cutting boomy resonances, damping a drum, gating decay, or high-passing rumble so notes and hits start and stop cleanly.
common_mistakes: Over-tightening with heavy gating so the low end sounds unnatural and choppy
Assuming tight always means better and stripping away useful sustain and warmth
Confusing a tight source with one that is simply thin or lacking low-end weight
scenario_contexts: A bass and kick are aligned and EQ'd so the low end sounds tight together
A boomy live-stage low end is tightened with high-pass filters and EQ cuts
A drum kit is damped and gated to give a tighter, more controlled sound

sources: Bobby Owsinski, The Mixing Engineer's Handbook

fields.definition: A studio and live-sound instruction to make a sound, usually the low end, more controlled and focused, for example by cutting boomy or excessive low frequencies, shortening reverb, damping resonance, or improving rhythmic timing.
fields.plain_english: This means making the low end more firm and controlled. You cut boomy low notes or shorten long echoes so the sound is clean.
fields.purpose_function: It directs the engineer to reduce looseness, boom or smear so the result sounds cleaner and more defined.
fields.practical_application: In response, a technician may high-pass rumble, cut a boomy resonance, gate a ringing drum, or shorten a long reverb tail to tighten the sound.
common_mistakes: Over-tightening until the sound loses natural weight and sustain
Only cutting lows when the real looseness is a timing or performance issue
Applying heavy gating that chops the sound unnaturally
scenario_contexts: A mix engineer is told to tighten up a boomy bass so it sits cleanly with the kick
A front-of-house engineer tightens up a loose, resonant stage low end
A producer asks to tighten up a ringing tom by damping and gating it

sources: Bobby Owsinski, The Mixing Engineer's Handbook
